source.authors: Bytheway JP, Price CJ, Banks PB
source.title: Deadly intentions: naïve introduced foxes show rapid attraction to odour cues of an unfamiliar native prey

value: foxes investigated significantly more sand plots with bandicoot (Perameles nasuta) odour than plots with black rat (Rattus rattus) odour or clean-towel control (chi-square 7.54, df 2, exact P = 0.024); more than 80 per cent of bandicoot plots investigated after two nights versus 17 per cent (rat) and 20 per cent (control)
units: categorical (number of sand plots investigated by foxes, Pearson chi-square across three odour treatments)
method: field sand-plot assay: sand monitoring plots (2 m wide, more than 500 m apart) raked daily; a towel pegged to the plot edge, first clean (familiarisation until fox interest in the clean towel declined) then carrying body, urine and faeces odour collected overnight on 20 x 30 cm towels placed in cage traps (bandicoot or black rat), or a clean towel (control); three treatment nights; a plot scored investigated if footprint counts, changes of direction or digging at the towel showed a fox investigation on any night; other fox activity scored as incidental passing
conditions: wild-sourced: free-living introduced red foxes on about 225 km2 of agricultural land and remnant mallee woodland at Walpeup, north-western Victoria, Australia, well outside the known ranges of both prey species (more than 300 km from the nearest bandicoot record; black rats rarely occur outside major rural centres such as Mildura); odour (body, urine, faeces) collected on towels in cage traps for one night at North Head, Sydney (page does not describe the donors' origin further); 72 plots built, foxes familiarised at 40; only plots familiarised and with fox activity on the treatment nights were analysed, n = 7 bandicoot, 12 rat, 10 control (the paper gives no reason for the other 11 plots); all plots received treatments on the same day, but how treatments were allocated to plots (randomised or not) is not described; plots monitored and re-raked daily for three days; individual foxes not identified, so plots rather than foxes are the unit and one fox may have visited several plots; same-section secondary result: rat odour plots (17 per cent) did not differ in rate from control plots (20 per cent), no separate rat versus control test printed; the authors call the bandicoot-over-rat result surprising and call their findings preliminary support; foxes came from an established population; run date not printed
where: Results, sand plot investigation by odour treatment
quote: Foxes investigated significantly more sand plots with bandicoot odours than sand plots with rat or control odours (Pearson Chi-Square X2 = 7.54, DF = 2 exact sig. (2-sided) P = 0.024, adjusted standardized residual of 2.7).
note: Classification: behavioural_response, choice of investigation at odour-bearing plots against an unscented control, with a heterospecific odour comparator; the value is limited to odour-driven plot investigation in the plot-level chi-square and is no individual-level threshold. Licence: the nature.com article page prints 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.' (publisher's own free full text). Byline as printed: Jenna P. Bytheway, Catherine J. Price & Peter B. Banks; Received 04 April 2016, Accepted 29 June 2016, Published 15 July 2016. source.authors: Dickman CR, Fardell LL, Hills N
source.title: Odour-mediated Interactions Between an Apex Reptilian Predator and its Mammalian Prey

value: sand goannas excavated artificial burrows containing small-mammal body odour significantly more often than odourless control burrows in both experimental phases; digs at odour burrows numbered 80 (Rattus villosissimus, 1365 burrow-days, phase 1), 88 (Sminthopsis youngsoni, 2028 burrow-days, phase 2), 79 (Notomys alexis) and 203 (Pseudomys hermannsburgensis) over a total of 3393 burrow-days, against 7 at control burrows over 3393 burrow-days
units: categorical (burrow excavation events per burrow-days, 1 burrow-day = 1 burrow over 1 day; generalised least squares (GLS) model comparison of odour versus odourless control burrows)
method: field artificial-burrow assay: clusters of four artificial burrows at 32 to 50 sites along bases or mid-sections of sand dunes; a small ball of cotton wool bearing the body odour of one small mammal species placed at the bottom of each of three burrows, fresh cotton wool in the fourth as odourless control; phase 1 odours of N. alexis, P. hermannsburgensis and R. villosissimus (September and November 2012), phase 2 with S. youngsoni replacing R. villosissimus (September 2013, April and November 2014); digs and tracks at burrows recorded as excavation events per burrow-day
conditions: wild-sourced: free-ranging sand goannas (Varanus gouldii) at three sites on Ethabuka Reserve, Queensland, Australia (Main Camp, Field River, Way Site); goannas in the study were captured by long-term live trapping or hand noosing for other parts of the study; a goanna removal programme (39 V. gouldii relocated more than 5 km away, September 2009 to November 2011) ran on about 50 ha at Main Camp before the burrow phases, and the paper does not say whether burrow sites lay in that area; small-mammal odour donors described as 'captive or wild-caught animals' without saying which; one fixed odourless control burrow per cluster, and the paper does not say whether odour placement within clusters was randomised; burrow-days: each odour treatment and the control ran 3393 burrow-days over both phases (1365 in phase 1, 2028 in phase 2); same-paper secondary and null results: goanna digging at P. hermannsburgensis burrows was not significantly higher than at R. villosissimus (phase 1, p = 0.748) or S. youngsoni (phase 2, p = 0.092) burrows; goannas dug less at N. alexis burrows than at the others; tracks were fewer at control burrows than at all other odour burrows except S. youngsoni, whose odour 'elicited very little response' (phase 2 tracks at S. youngsoni versus control p = 0.8444); tracks at 164 odour burrows versus 29 at control (Discussion); digs are pooled counts for the goanna population at each cluster, not per animal
quote: Model results showed that V. gouldii excavated burrows containing small mammal odour significantly more often than the odourless control burrows in both phase 1 and phase 2 (Table 2, Fig. 2).
note: Classification: behavioural_response, excavation of burrows bearing prey odour against odourless control burrows in the field; the value says goannas dig at odour burrows and does not establish which compound is the cue; the track measure did not separate S. youngsoni odour from the control.
